771.dq: Within words, primary stress is generally predictable. Secondary stress is noted in longer utterances, but has not been analyzed.
771.dloc: Carlson 1972 sec. 1.1 (p. 2) and sec. 2.21-2.212 (pp. 24-26); Bates & Carlson WPLC sec. 2.1
771.heavy: none: no syllable-weight criterion; stress is assigned by morpheme stress class (inherently-stressed / variable-stress / unstressed suffixes; stress-retentive vs stress-shifting roots). ST1's 'strong roots, strong suffixes' is diacritic morphological strength, not phonological weight.
771.dflt: not applicable (no weight criterion); a bare or prefixed-only root carries the stress
771.prule: Morpheme-class hierarchy: an inherently-stressed (strong) suffix takes primary stress; otherwise a stress-retentive (strong) root keeps it; otherwise the (rightmost) variable-stress suffix takes it from a stress-shifting (weak) root; a root alone or with prefixes only is stressed on the root; prefixes and unstressed suffixes never bear stress; unstressed vowels are then deleted (Carlson 1972: two ordered rules, stress assignment then vowel deletion). Bates & Carlson restate it as the hierarchy strong suffixes > strong roots > variable suffixes > weak roots > weak suffixes.
771.srule: None distinctive: 'There is no distinctive secondary stress' (Carlson & Bates 1990 p. 73, 1991 p. 37); 'unlike some related languages in having no secondary stress' (Bates & Carlson 1989 p. 75); 'Each word has one main stress' (Carlson & Esling 2000 p. 99). Carlson 1972 sec. 1.1 had noted secondary stress 'in longer utterances' as unanalysed; his derivational 'secondary stress rule' (sec. 2.2432) is deleted before the surface.

evidence_works.detail: Black diagnoses the two root classes by primary-stress placement over a data set of 'nearly 6000 non-compound forms' (fn. 1, p. 77); the examples are from the Carlson & Flett 1989 Spokane Dictionary unless otherwise indicated (fn. 3, p. 77), otherwise from her own fieldnotes (Black 1995) or Carlson & Thompson 1982, and data-set forms cited in the footnotes are also attributed to Carlson & Bates 1990 (fns. 13, 15): 'The facts of primary stress assignment indicate that there are two types of Root in Spokane: strong and weak. Black 1996 finds that the most reliable way to determine the strong or weak status of a Root is to check whether or not the Root vowel bears primary stress when the Root is followed by certain grammatical suffixes. Such suffixes include m Middle, Out-of-Control reduplication, mi Nonperfective and numerous subject and object person markers, among many others. In the event that the Root vowel does bear primary stress in such a context, then it is identified as a strong Root; otherwise, it is identified as a weak Root.' (sec. 2.0, p. 77). Paradigms (1)-(10), pp. 78-79, show strong roots keeping stress on the root vowel and weak roots losing it to the suffix. Refinement: against 'Numerous accounts, including Bates and Carlson (1989) and Carlson and Bates (1990)' which locate the strong/weak difference solely in morphological properties (end of sec. 2.0, pp. 79-80), namely the lexical diacritics [+ stressable] and [+ strong] (fn. 4, p. 80), she argues 'these accounts miss an important generalization' (p. 80): the stressed vowel of a weak root matches the stressed epenthetic vowel in every environment (secs. 3.1-3.2, pp. 80-82), so 'Black 1996 provides an analysis of this strong/weak distinction among Roots where the stressed Root vowel of a weak Root is not identified as underlying /i,u,e,o, or a/, but rather as a phonologically conditioned realization of the vowel schwa' (sec. 3.3, p. 83). Also notes one root, kʷen, that shows 'both strong and weak stress behaviors' (fn. 10, p. 81) and that the class of many roots 'has yet to be determined' (fn. 1, p. 77).

dfl.note: The elsewhere position is the root: a root alone or with prefixes only carries primary stress, and stress-retentive roots keep it under suffixation unless an inherently-stressed suffix is present; stress lands on a suffix only via the morpheme-class hierarchy. Roots (and most morphemes) are monosyllabic CVC, so no root-initial/-final edge is stated; Bates & Carlson p. 78: 'The basic generalization about Spokane is that roots carry stress... Spokane morphemes are usually monosyllabic...…
dfl.q: A Spokan word has the following structure: (PREFIXES) ROOT (SUFFIXES) A root may occur alone to form a word. When it does, it naturally takes primary stress. When prefixes are added, the root still has primary stress. When suffixes are added, primary stress may occur on the root or on one of the suffixes.

772.dq: Por razón del lugar que ocupa en cada caso la sílaba acentuada, existen en español tres clases de palabras: agudas, con el acento de intensidad sobre la última sílaba ...; llanas, con el acento sobre la penúltima ..., y esdrújulas, con el acento sobre la antepenúltima (Navarro Tomás 1918 §154); §158 separately treats words that are 'débiles' (unstressed) in the phrase.
772.dloc: Navarro Tomás 1918 §§153-156, pp. 139-140 (Gibson 2011 pp. 3-4, 9-10 for the weight discussion)
772.heavy: Navarro Tomás states no weight criterion; the only segmental conditioning is orthographic/word-final: unmarked words ending in a consonant other than n, s are final-stressed, words ending in a vowel or n, s are penult-stressed. Gibson 2011 reports Harris (1983) as treating closed (bimoraic, CVC/CVG) syllables as heavy ('Stress heavy (bimoraic) syllables') and disputes that weight is active in Modern Spanish.
772.dflt: penult (trochaic default; vowel-final words); consonant-final words default to final
772.prule: Word stress (acento de intensidad) is lexically given and contrastive (límite / limite / limité), confined to the last three syllables of the word (agudas, llanas, esdrújulas; sobresdrújulas only with enclitics). Defaults by word ending: vowel/-n/-s final -> penult; other consonant-final -> final; all departures are marked in the orthography. Gibson 2011 (Núñez Cedeño & Morales-Front counts over 91,000 non-verbs): V-final 88% penult, 11.1% antepenult, 0.87% final; C-final 97.8% final, 2.03% penult, 0.05% antepenult.
772.srule: Non-contrastive rhythmic prominence ('acento rítmico'): Navarro Tomás 1918 §163 hears, tentatively, an alternating rise and fall among the unstressed syllables counted from the stressed syllable (levels 2-1-3 repetir, 3-1-2 rápido, 1-3-1-2 retórica, 2-1-3-1 abadesa, 2-1-2-1-3-1 contraproducente), i.e. weaker prominences on alternate syllables away from the tonic; he says its nature and principles are not well known. Later work (Hualde 2007, 2010) treats these secondary stresses as optional postlexical prominences of emphatic/didactic style, placed two syllables before the tonic or on the word-initial syllable, with stress clash not avoided (rùmános); RAE 2011 §9.1r: alternate syllables (binary feet) leftward from the primary, or word-initial.

morph.rootq: ADJUDICATED 'no' (A 'partly', B 'no'). Neither source states the accent rule with reference to the root/stem; both give a word-level, right-edge, lexically specified accent within a final three-syllable window. Navarro Tomás 1918 §154 (p.139): 'existen en español tres clases de palabras: agudas, con el acento de intensidad sobre la última sílaba ...; llanas, con el acento sobre la penúltima ..., y esdrújulas, con el acento sobre la antepenúltima ... morph.elicq: Navarro Tomás 1918 states no elicitation procedure; the description is a native phonetician's account covering words in isolation and in the phrase, judged by ear: §162 (p.147) 'Cualquiera que sea la combinación en que las palabras aparezcan dentro de la frase, su acento se mantiene de un modo invariable sobre la misma sílaba en que lo llevan aisladamente consideradas; pero suelen darse diferencias en cuanto al grado de intensidad entre las diversas sílabas fuertes de una misma frase.' §163 (rhythmic/secondary accent): 'No conocemos suficientemente la naturaleza del acento rítmico ...; sin embargo, en series silábicas de cierta extensión, el oído, por lo que al acento se refiere, cree…

773.dq: The most superficial observation about Catalan stress is that words are either unstressed, or else stressed on one of the last three syllables. ... Polymorphemic words show only one stress on the surface, the position being determined by the inherent properties of their constituent morphemes.
773.dloc: ch. 1 'The Accentual System', sec. 1 pp. 19-20; sec. 3 p. 26; sec. 4 pp. 33-34 (thesis pagination)
773.heavy: No weight criterion stated as such. The rule-based alternative Mascaró reviews (Wheeler 1974) stresses the vowel before the word-final segment, i.e. final stress when the word ends in a consonant (closed final syllable), penultimate when it ends in a vowel; StressTyp2 recodes this as 'final if heavy' with Heavy = closed syllable (lexical marking). Vowel length plays no role (no long vowels).
773.dflt: penultimate (V-final words are mostly paroxytone) -- as a statistical default only
773.prule: Stress is lexical (underlying property of morphemes) confined to the last three syllables of the word; word stress = the rightmost underlyingly stressed morpheme (Destressing removes the others); 'prestressed' suffixes (e.g. -ic) put stress on the preceding syllable. Statistically oxytones > paroxytones > proparoxytones; the Wheeler-type default (stress the vowel preceding the final segment: C-final words oxytone, V-final words paroxytone) needs diacritics [+/-E] and still fails for V-final oxytones (cafè, sofà, ximpanzé) and many proparoxytones (dèficit, Júpiter).
773.srule: None at word level: 'Polymorphemic words show only one stress on the surface' (p.19); Destressing accounts for 'the monoaccented character of words, simple or compound' (p.50); compound and prefixed-word first members keep an unreduced vowel but are perceptually unstressed (sec. 6 p.43, Appendix I pp.148-150); a secondary stress only on the first word of a two-word phrase ('in X##Y, X has a secondary stress', p.78).

On the Notion of Theme Vowel: A New Approach to Catalan Verbal Morphology. MS thesis, MIT (hdl 1721.1/9532) (verb template Root-Th-T-Agr, stress ch.5); Carbonell & Llisterri (1992) 'Catalan'…
morph.rootq: Mascaró 1976 pp.35-36: "A verb form has a stem consisting of a root, possibly with derivational affixes, and a thematic vowel. The stem is followed by tense markers, and these by person markers (in the finite forms). Under the present system the stress should fall on the root when no stressed suffixes follow, and on the last stressed suffix if there are any." Also p.20: "Most inflectional suffixes are unstressed. Thus the feminine marker a, the masculine marker u and most verbal suffixes don't bear or affect stress. A few verbal flexion markers, however, are stressed. ... Prefixes never affect the stress of the stem, and can be unstressed or stressed." and p.34: "If there are several…
morph.elicq: Isolated citation forms from the author's own Barcelona Catalan, method otherwise unstated: "I have used the dialectal variety of Catalan spoken in Barcelona as the source for my data." (Mascaró 1976 Preface p.3); "To take the simplest cases, consider a few monomorphemic words with no or zero flexion marks" (p.19); forms cited as "the phonetic form of these words in isolation" (p.101). Plus a perception experiment for non-main stress (Appendix I, pp.148-150): "A list of 36 words or phrases containing pairs of homonyms was recorded in random order, and three subjects were asked to identify each word with two written choices, one being the word read, the other its homonym."
morph.stmt: Catalan inflection and derivation are suffixal -- "A verb form has a stem consisting of a root, possibly with derivational affixes, and a thematic vowel. The stem is followed by tense markers, and these by person markers" (Mascaró 1976:35); nominal feminine -a / plural -s, diminutive -ɛt, nominalisers -dor/-ció/-ment and verbaliser -itz- are all suffixes -- while the only pre-root material is a small set of derivational prefixes (in-, des-, mal-, en-; "Prefixes never affect the stress of the stem", p.20) and the unstressed proclitics (articles, object/reflexive pronouns, which become enclitic only on infinitives, gerunds and imperatives: Bonet 1991:124).

773.cfw: Mascaró 1976, the Institut d'Estudis Catalans grammar of 2016, Faust & Torres-Tamarit 2017 and Torres-Tamarit & Pons-Moll 2019 all place Catalan word stress on one of the last three syllables, contrastive and not fully predictable though with a strong default of final stress in consonant-final and penultimate stress in vowel-final nouns, and no source disagrees.

evidence_works.work: Torres-Tamarit & Pons-Moll 2019, Enclitic-induced stress shift in Catalan (Journal of Linguistics 55: 407-444)
evidence_works.independence: first-hand
evidence_works.note: Data: previous literature for Barcelona Catalan (Bonet 1992, 1995, 2002) plus the authors' own interviews with 3 speakers from Mallorca, Menorca and Formentera, elicited by a Spanish-to-Catalan translation task and a situational questionnaire (p. 5). Findings: under enclisis Barcelona Catalan preserves the stress of the isolated verb ('namely, there is no stress shift', p. 6), so the verb-enclitic group can be proparoxytone or pre-proparoxytone; Formentera Catalan shifts stress to the last syllable of the group when it ends in a consonant and to the penultimate when it ends in a vowel; Mallorca and Menorca Catalan shift it to the last syllable; in the shifting varieties 'the verbal base does not carry stress, either primary or secondary, as evidenced by vowel reduction' (p. 7; same statement for Mallorca/Menorca p. 9). The paper restates the unmarked nominal pattern the record's cfw already carries (vowel-final paroxytone, consonant-final oxytone, about 86% of inflected word forms after Serra 1996), says 'the position of stress is not always predictable' (p. 10), cites Mascaró (1976) for stress being 'specified underlyingly for each lexical item' (p. 13), and adopts an analysis with 'no alternating stresses' (p. 13).

evidence_works.work: Ortega-Llebaria & Prieto 2011, Acoustic correlates of stress in Central Catalan and Castilian Spanish (Language and Speech 54: 73-97)
evidence_works.independence: first-hand
evidence_works.note: Production experiment. Measured: F0, segment and syllable duration, overall intensity and spectral tilt (secs. 2.4.1-2.4.4, pp. 80-81) on 15 stress-minimal pairs of four-syllable verbs in -minar/-nimar with cognates in both languages, paroxytone present (determino) versus oxytone past (determinó), read in accented and in deaccented reporting-clause contexts (sec. 2.1, pp. 77-78; Appendix A p. 95). Speakers: ten native speakers of Central Catalan (all female, aged 20-32) and ten of Castilian Spanish (sec. 2.3, p. 80). Findings: 'Duration was a consistent stress correlate in all vowels in both languages, regardless of their formant frequency differences across stress contexts and of the absence of pitch accents' and 'changes in spectral tilt were significant only in Catalan and in those vowels that alternate a more open and peripheral realization in stressed syllables with a mid-central realization in unstressed syllables' (abstract, p. 73); 'Catalan and Spanish speakers consistently express the stress contrast in unaccented contexts as well as in accented sentences' and 'stressed syllables were significantly longer than unstressed syllables in both accented and unaccented sentences' (sec. 4, p. 90). Bears on the phonetic realization of the contrastive stress the record codes, not on placement, secondary stress, domain or exceptions.

evidence_works.work: Faust & Torres-Tamarit 2017, Stress and final /n/ deletion in Catalan: Combining Strict CV and OT (Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 2(1): 63, 1-23. doi:10.5334/gjgl.64)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article describes Catalan word stress as regular (final in consonant-final words, penultimate in vowel-final words, a right-aligned trochaic foot) or lexical (any vowel inside a right-edge three-syllable window), and words whose final /n/ deletes take final stress like consonant-final words. The catalog entry has kind 'lexical' with an empty rule field, so the article agrees that stress is partly lexical and supplies the default rule and the three-syllable window; it is a theoretical (Strict CV + OT) analysis using dictionary forms, with no acoustic measurements.
evidence_works.loc: p. 7, section 2.2 'Stress in Catalan' (Art. 63); stress algorithm (13) p. 8 and (15) p. 9
evidence_works.venue: Glossa: a journal of general linguistics

evidence_works.work: Prieto & Maria del Mar Vanrell 2010, The relevance of prosodic structure in tonal articulation: edge effects at the prosodic word level in Catalan and Spanish (Journal of Phonetics [vol/issue/pages not in packet]. doi:10.1016/j.wocn.2010.10.004)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: An intonation study on five Central Catalan speakers: the pitch accent on a stressed syllable starts low at that syllable and peaks in the following syllable, and the peak comes about 35 ms earlier when the stressed syllable is word-final (oxytones like comprà) than when it is penultimate (paroxytones like compraven); listeners use this timing to tell such minimal pairs apart. It takes the lexical final-vs-penultimate stress contrast as given and does not state a stress rule; stressed-syllable duration showed no consistent word-edge effect.
evidence_works.loc: accepted manuscript (UNED e-spacio, 44 pp.), pp. 5, 7, 13-14, 18-19, 34; page numbers are the manuscript's own

774.dq: (25) English Stress Rule: At the right edge of a word, form a maximally binary foot on the rhyme projection ... Label feet s w. (p. 238) ... Notice that the last expression, with a branching final foot, is highly aberrant within the English word stress system, suggesting perhaps that the phenomenon is phrasal in nature, and not to be included within the word stress rules. (p. 264)
774.dloc: pp. 237-240, sections 2.1-2.2, rules (24) Consonant Extrametricality, (25) English Stress Rule, (30) Long Vowel Stressing, (33) Noun Extrametricality; exx. (23), (28), (29), (32)
774.heavy: Nonfinally: branching rhyme = long vowel (incl. diphthong; LP's long/short vowel division, p. 237) or closed syllable is heavy ('any C0VC sequence preceding /yVn/ or /yos/ will count as a closed syllable, and thus receive stress just like any other heavy penult', p. 267; exx. (32) agenda, appendix, amalgam alongside Arizona, factotum, elitist, p. 239). Word-finally the criterion differs by category: verbs/unsuffixed adjectives need a long vowel or a final string of at least two consonants (single final consonant extrametrical by (24)); in nouns a final long vowel is always stressed (Long Vowel Stressing (30)), the final rhyme otherwise being extrametrical (33), with short-vowel final stress 'lexically idiosyncratic' (29).
774.dflt: antepenult in nouns (America), penult in verbs/unsuffixed adjectives (develop, common): the maximal binary foot at the right edge after extrametricality
774.prule: English Stress Rule (25): at the right edge of the word build a maximally binary, quantity-sensitive, left-headed foot whose weak member must be a light (nonbranching) rhyme, after Consonant Extrametricality (24) for all words and Noun (and Adjective) Extrametricality (33) marking the final rhyme extrametrical. Net: verbs/unsuffixed adjectives = final if -VV(C)/-VCC else penult; nouns (and suffixed adjectives) = penult if heavy else antepenult, with a final long vowel always stressed (30) and main stress then normally on the rightmost nonfinal foot. Output is lexically listed; Hayes states the rules hold 'generally' with lexically idiosyncratic final stressing (29) and exception classes.
774.srule: Strong Retraction (Hayes 1982, rule (43)): to the left of the main-stress foot, remaining syllables are footed right-to-left into maximally disyllabic, quantity-insensitive trochaic (s w) feet whose heads bear secondary stress, i.e. on alternate syllables counted leftward from the main-stress foot (Apalachicola: even-numbered syllables from the end; hamamelidanthemum: odd-numbered; designate, coruscate: initial binary foot 'without regard to syllable quantity'). Weak feet are then removed by Prestress, Sonorant and Poststress Destressing (initial light syllable unstressed: Connecticut; an initial ternary stretch when the final foot is strongest: abracadabra, Winnepesaukee, but binary before a weak final foot: Saskatchewan, Mamaroneck). Nouns also keep a final secondary stress from Long Vowel Stressing (30) or a lexical final foot (cavalcade, misanthrope, Hackensack). In derived words secondary stresses preserve the base's stresses cyclically (fraternization vs compurgation).

morph.src: Main source: Sweet, Henry. 1891 [t.p. 1892]. A New English Grammar, Logical and Historical. Part I: Introduction, Phonology, and Accidence. Oxford: Clarendon Press (archive.org public-domain scan newenglishgramma01sweeuoft in the copy consulted). Secondary source: Hayes, Bruce. 1982. Extrametricality and English Stress. Linguistic Inquiry 13(2): 227-276 (author-hosted PDF + in the copy consulted; StressTyp2's source) for the stress description and its evidence base; Anderson et al. 2022, Essentials of Linguistics 2nd ed. (eCampusOntario Pressbooks, CC BY-NC-SA), ch. 5.2, 5.6, 5.7, as modern corroboration of the inflectional inventory.
morph.rootq: Sweet 1891 §881: 'The OE principle of putting the stress on the first syllable of a word generally resulted in the principal stress being on the root-syllable of inflected or derived words. This principle is still maintained in MnE in native words, as in fearful, fearfully, fearless, fearlessness, fisher, fishery, fisherman.' §883: 'Native words which had weak stress on the first syllable in OE and ME, such as arise, become, forgive, to-day, still keep this stress in MnE, as also those French words which preserved a similar stress in ME through their resemblance to the above native words, such as avow, defend.' But §884: 'There are many foreign derivative endings ... which regularly take…
morph.elicq: Hayes 1982 (the StressTyp source) argues from lexical citation forms and pronouncing-dictionary entries: 'all the words under (91a) are marked with final main stress in Kenyon and Knott (1944)' (p.262); 'There is naturally a great deal of variation among speakers; for the dialect of Kenyon and Knott (1944) we find: (99) a. Invariant [i]: memorabilia ...' (p.266); 'This can be determined by consulting the entries in Walker's dictionary' (p.272); plus native-speaker judgments of isolated nonce words ('forms like podectal and ponitode ... sound strange to native speakers', p.237). Sweet 1891 states no elicitation method…
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing: 'As inflection is mainly final in English and the other languages cognate with it... there is a tendency to restrict the term inflection to final additions to a word' (Sweet 1891 §74); all living inflections are suffixal -s (plural, genitive group-clitic, 3sg), -ed/-t/-d, -ing, -en, -er/-est (§73, §1000, §1289; 'the consonantal inflections being the only living or productive ones' §1287); derivation uses both prefixes (un-, be-, mis-; dis-, re-, in-, en-, counter-) and the far more numerous category-changing suffixes…

evidence_works.independence: first-hand

evidence_works.work: Nida 1960, A synopsis of English syntax (Norman: SIL of the University of Oklahoma, Linguistic Series 4: pp. 67-68, 80)
evidence_works.independence: first-hand
evidence_works.detail: Syntactic synopsis; the stress facts rest on the author's own speech ('This pattern is almost always maintained in the writer's speech', p. 67) with contrast pairs (a 'Chinese 'bank vs a Chin'ese in'vasion; the 'fourteen 'boys vs He was four'teen). Adds two phrase-level points the entry does not carry: (i) 'Certain multisyllable primary attributives accented on the final syllable in absolute or post-verb position, may be accented on a non-final syllable when immediately preceding a subject-head accented on a first syllable' (p. 67; list all-wise, biting-cold,... Chinese, fourteen... unknown, well-done, well-made, wide-open), with 'Before subject-heads with initial unstressed syllable the choice of accentual forms varies' (pp. 67-68); (ii) 'Many determiners are often atonic, and except in the case of emphatic or contrastive stress do not constitute the intonation "peg" or "peak" of the subject-head expression... The following determiners are often atonic. my, our, your, his, her, its, their, the, a' (p. 80). No word-level placement rule; nothing bears on kind, rule, secondary stress or domain.

evidence_works.work: Brilioth 1913, A grammar of the dialect of Lorton (Cumberland): historical and descriptive (Oxford: Oxford University Press: §244 p. 67, p. 130, §406 p. 104)
evidence_works.independence: first-hand
evidence_works.detail: Descriptive-historical dialect grammar of Lorton (West Cumberland), not the standard variety the entry codes. Adds: (i) stress-conditioned vowel reduction split by level, '§ 244. Short and long vowels as well as diphthongs in unaccented syllables have been weakened into ə, i, or disappeared altogether. These weakenings may be divided into two different groups: A. Weakenings caused by word-stress; B. Weakenings caused by sentence-stress. To the former group belong chiefly prefixes and suffixes as well as initial, medial, and final syllables preceded or followed by the principal accent; to the latter enclitic and proclitic words, articles, pronouns, particles, prepositions, and auxiliaries' (p. 67); (ii) two suffix-stressed adverbs, 'Adverbs of manner and degree. Two of these adverbs have the stress on the adverbial suffix: [əkɔːdənlai] accordingly, [siuərlai] surely (this pronunciation is now only heard from old people)' (p. 130); (iii) pronouns with 'secondary and unstressed forms' (§406, p. 104). No placement rule; nothing bears on kind, rule, secondary stress or domain.

evidence_works.work: Hirst 1906, A grammar of the dialect of Kendal (Westmoreland), descriptive and historical (Heidelberg: Winter: §12 p. 8, p. 12, §95 p. 46)
evidence_works.independence: first-hand
evidence_works.detail: Dialect grammar of the country around Kendal, South Westmorland, from one informant (Roger Capstick), not the standard variety the entry codes. Adds that the dialect distinguishes main and secondary stress and lists stress-conditioned segmental alternations: '§ 12. o (ɔ) the mid-back-wide-round only occurs in syllables which have not the main stress. In studied speech it passes into [ʊ] the high-back-wide. Examples: wino vb. winnow, hwar ðə ko frə where they come from' (p. 8); 'In addition to the above consonants, the stress h exists in Kendal, but does not occur in cases where original stress has been lost' (p. 12); '§ 95. ME. u from OE. u and a has passed into a in the words kad could, ʃad should, masl sb. mussel... In the first two cases, the unrounding is due to secondary stress' (p. 46). No placement rule; nothing bears on kind, rule, sec_rule or domain.

evidence_works.work: Wright 1892, A grammar of the dialect of Windhill, in the West Riding of Yorkshire (London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner: §3 p. 3, §353 p. 122, §399 p. 166, Notes p. 212)
evidence_works.independence: first-hand
evidence_works.detail: Descriptive grammar of the Windhill (West Riding) dialect, not the standard variety the entry codes. Adds partial stress facts, no general placement rule: 'All the diphthongs and triphthongs have the stress on the first element' (p. 3); reflexive pronouns misen, ðisen, isen, wəsen etc.: 'The stress is always on the second syllable. When these pronouns are used emphatically the stress on the second syllable is of course stronger than when they are used reflexively' (§353, p. 122); 'The adverbs of manner mostly end in -li, as ādli hardly, oekədli awkwardly; but we have the stress on the suffix in siuəlĭ surely, əkuədinlái accordingly' (§399, p. 166); notation 'The (·) denotes that the following syllable has the strong stress, thus asem·ive (I. 3), ·aim (I. 4)' (Notes, p. 212). Nothing bears on kind, rule, secondary stress or domain.

evidence_works.work: Özçelik 2016, The Prosodic Acquisition Path Hypothesis: Towards explaining variability in L2 acquisition of phonology (Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 1(1): 28, 1-48. doi:10.5334/gjgl.47)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The English section is a textbook summary built on Kager 1989 and Hayes 1982 (the catalog's own source): nouns take antepenultimate stress when the penult is light and penultimate stress otherwise, verbs make only the final consonant extrametrical, and secondary stresses fall on right-to-left binary weight-sensitive trochees. It reports no new English data and matches the catalog's Latin-type noun rule, verb rule and alternating secondary stress.
evidence_works.loc: sec. 2.1 'English stress', pp. 4-8, exx. (1)-(15), parameter summary (15) p. 8; secondary stress and Iterativity exx. (8)-(9) pp. 6-7
evidence_works.venue: Glossa: a journal of general linguistics

evidence_works.work: Vander Klok & Michael Wagner 2018, Prosodic focus in English vs (French: A scope account. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 3(1): 71, 1-47. doi:10.5334/gjgl.1)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article is about phrase-level focus prominence, not word-stress placement: it states in passing that English accentuation is a property of words and that focus marking is stress-based, and it measures how focused vs given words differ in pitch, intensity and duration. 775.dq: Each word has a primary stress, which, in the regular case, comes from a word-final trochee. There is also an optional secondary stress at the beginning of the word, which is claimed to come from a word-initial trochee. Hence, a German word has at most two stresses, one final and one initial.

775.heavy: Féry: heavy = CVVC (long tense vowel + closing consonant) and CVCC (lax vowel + two closing consonants); light = CVC, CVV, CV; superlight = schwa/syllabic-sonorant syllables (never stressed): hierarchy 'CVCC, CVVC > CVC, CVV, CV > Cə'. A closed (non-superlight) penult blocks retraction to the antepenult. Jessen (StressTyp2 carried passage): 'Unequivocally, a closed syllable counts as heavy'; final syllable regularly stressed if long vowel + >=1 coda C or short vowel + >=2 coda Cs; status of long vowels as heavy 'not completely clear'.
775.dflt: penult (trochaic default); antepenult only if penult is a schwa syllable
775.prule: Word-final trochee: main stress on the final syllable if it is heavy (superheavy CVVC/CVCC), otherwise on the penult; antepenult when the penult is a schwa syllable (and, exceptionally/lexically, in words with an open penult); schwa syllables never stressed; main stress confined to the last three (full) syllables of a non-derived word. Exceptions (final stress on light syllables, penult stress with heavy final, antepenult stress with open penult) are lexically prespecified.
775.srule: Optional secondary stress on the word-initial syllable (word-initial trochee), not realized when it would clash with main stress (main stress on the second syllable); footing not exhaustive, so at most two stresses per word in the regular case; in words of more than four syllables an additional optional rhythmic stress may fall on every other syllable counted from either edge (Mèteorologíe ~ Mèteòrologíe ~ Mèteoròlogíe, fn. 2). Not weight-driven.

775.sec_quote: There is also an optional secondary stress at the beginning of the word, which is claimed to come from a word-initial trochee. Hence, a German word has at most two stresses, one final and one initial. Stress clashes are avoided, which means that the initial stress is only realized when the word is long enough to have an unstressed syllable between the initial and the final stress.
775.sec_loc: ROA-301 p.3 (Introduction); pp.10-11 with ex. (9a-b); p.39 sec. 5 Conclusion; p.42 fn. 2

st.weight_quote: Open syllables, which always have a tense vowel in their nucleus, as well as syllables with a lax vowel and a single closing consonant or glide, are light. Syllables with a tense vowel and a closing consonant and those with a lax vowel and two closing consonants are heavy. In short, the heavy syllables have an additional consonant as compared to the light ones.

evidence_works.work: Sauerland 1994, German diathesis and verb morphology (Verb Classes and Alternations in Bangla, German, English, and Korean, MIT AI Memo 1517 / CBCL Memo 137: 50-68)
evidence_works.independence: first-hand
evidence_works.detail: Adds morphological detail outside the entry's monomorphemic domain: inseparable verbal prefixes (be-, ver-, zer-,...) are unstressed and separable particles (an-, auf-, um-,...) are stressed; be-prefixation generally presupposes a verb root with initial stress. p. 54 fn. 4: 'Since the prefixation of be- is in general only possible – there are some lexicalized exceptions – if the verb root has initial stress, verbs that don't satisfy this constraint are enclosed in brackets in the following list.' p. 65: 'The inseparable prefixes are destressed, the separable particles are stressed. In infinite clauses with zu (to) the zu goes between the verb and a seperable prefix, but before an inseparable prefix.' and 'Generally the prefixation of a verb that doesn't have initial stress is illformed, so the constraint against the multiple prefixation with two inseparable prefixes.'.
evidence_works.venue: MIT AI Lab memo (working paper collection)

evidence_works.work: Vennemann 1991, Skizze der deutschen Wortprosodie (Zeitschrift für Sprachwissenschaft 10: 86-111)
evidence_works.independence: first-hand
evidence_works.detail: States the same right-edge, weight-hedged system as the entry, as a set of rules and defaults for simplex words. p. 97: '[Rl] Vollsilbenregel (Full syllable rule): Nur Vollsilben können akzentuiert werden.' (= schwa never stressed). p. 98: '[R 2] Reduktionssilbenregel (Reduced syllable rule): Eine bedeckte reduzierte Ultima arretiert den Akzent auf der letzten Vollsilbe.' (= final covered schwa syllable -> penult) and '[R 3] Dreisilbenregel (Three syllable rule): Nur die drei letzten Vollsilben eines unzusammengesetzten Wortes können akzentuiert werden.' p. 99: 'R 3 bringt zum Ausdruck, daß das heutige Standarddeutsch einen Finalakzent hat, der als Ultimal-, Pänultimal- oder Antepänultimalakzent in Erscheinung tritt.' and '[R4] Pänultimaregel (Heavy penult rule): Der Akzent geht nicht über eine schwere Pänultima zurück.' (= antepenult only over a light penult). p. 101: '[Nl] Normalitätsbeziehung für schwere Ultimae (Heavy ultima default): Simplicia mit schwerer Ultima werden auf der Ultima akzentuiert, insbesondere wenn diese mehrfach geschlossen ist.' p. 102: '[N 2] Normalitätsbeziehung für leichte Ultimae (Light ultima default): Simplicia mit leichter Ultima werden nicht auf der Ultima akzentuiert.' p. 103: '[N 4] Normalitätsbeziehung für Pänultimae (Penult Default): Ist keine andere Normalitätsbeziehung (und keine Regel) einschlägig, so wird die Pänultima akzentuiert.' Differences of detail, not of coding: (a) weight is defined more broadly than Féry's CVVC/CVCC class, p. 97: 'Eine Vollsilbe heißt leicht im Standarddeutschen, wenn sie offen, monophthongisch und sanft geschnitten ist; andernfalls heißt sie schwer im Standarddeutschen.' so a closed, diphthongal or sharply-cut (short-vowel) syllable counts as heavy, and the N1 default is strongest for multiply closed ultimas (Féry's superheavy class); (b) the N-relations are explicitly defaults with listed exceptions, not rules ('Es geht hier also nicht um strenge Regeln, sondern um Bevorzugungszusammenhänge', p. 101); exceptions to R4 are names and compound-like words, p. 100 fn. 19: 'Übrigens gibt es Ausnahmen. Sie erscheinen vor allem in zwei Gruppen. Die erste enthält Namen: 'Tu.ran.dot, 'Va.len.tin, 'Au.gus.tin.'... 'Die zweite Gruppe enthält Wörter, die sich wie Komposita „anfühlen"'; (c) on secondary prominence the paper only separates accentuability from rhythmic prominence, p. 88 fn. 5: 'Man muß natürlich zwischen Akzentuierbarkeit und rhythmischer Hervorhebbarkeit unterscheiden. Eine Reduktionssilbe kann nicht akzentuiert werden, sie kann aber metrisch durchaus prominent werden (einen „Nebenakzent" erhalten)', and p. 103 speaks of vowel reduction 'zwischen zwei rhythmischen Prominenzstellen, etwa Wortakzentstelle und rhythmischer Nebenakzentstelle'; it gives no rule for the placement of secondary stress, so the entry's sec fields (Féry's optional initial secondary) are untouched. 101 ('Normalit tsbeziehung f r', 'Bevorzugungszusammenh nge') and in fn. 5 on p. 88 ('naturlich'), prints 'Füll syllable rule' for 'Full syllable rule' on p. 97 and '„Nebenakzent44' for '„Nebenakzent"' on p. 89, and hyphenates 'Simpli-/cia' (p. 102) and 'Pänulti-/ma' (p. 103) across lines; the quotes above restore these.

evidence_works.work: Tomaschek & Domahs 2023, Modelling German Word Stress (Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 8(1): 1-28. doi:10.16995/glossa.9015)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: A two-layer network predicts the stress position of German words from their phoneme or grapheme trigrams with about 90% accuracy, better than from abstract cues such as syllable count and weight, and the authors find no evidence for a default stress position. evidence_works.work: Kaland 2024, When recall gets stressful: comparing Papuan Malay and German listeners' lexical storage of word stress (Laboratory Phonology 15(1): 1-27. doi:10.16995/labphon.11695)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: German serves as the free-stress control: its listeners recalled stress patterns well (mean index 10.51, in line with earlier German studies), which the author reads as lexical storage of stress. corr.head: StressTyp2 codes a weight-sensitive pattern that later instrumental studies dispute
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Malay: In words of three or more syllables, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy, else on the antepenultimate syllable if it is heavy, else on the antepenultimate syllable. In words of two or fewer syllables, primary stress falls on the…". StressTyp2 cites Winstedt (1927 edition) and Lewis 1947 for this coding, which matches Winstedt's own rule (penult; final when the penult is an open ĕ syllable) only in part. The instrumental descriptions followed here (Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008; Clynes & Deterding 2011: 265) find no word stress, so the language is classed as having no word stress and is not counted in the weight-pattern census.

ev.cite: Winstedt, R.O. 1913. Malay Grammar. Oxford: Clarendon Press. (1st edition; StressTyp2 cites the 1927 2nd edition of the same work.) archive.org id malaygrammar00winsrich. — Section 14 'Accent', p.31 (PDF leaf 35)
ev.text: Ordinarily in the Malay word, the accent falls on the penultimate except that (1) when the penultimate is ĕ in an open syllable and rarely in a closed, then the accent falls on the last syllable, ĕnám, tĕngáh; (2) when a derivative is built up by prefixes from a monosyllabic root, the accent sometimes remains on that root, namely, on the last syllable; (3) in the vocative, the stress is sometimes thrown on the last syllable.

contra.head: An earlier description states a penultimate accent rule (superseded)
contra.detail: Winstedt 1913 (Malay Grammar, sec. 14 'Accent', pp. 30-32) gives the accent as ordinarily penultimate, on the last syllable when the penult is ĕ (schwa) in an open syllable, while noting that 'there is no strong accent on any syllable in a Malay word'. Superseded classification: weight-sensitive, with qualifications (full vs. reduced vowel). Against it, the classification followed here: Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008 sec. 10 ('We therefore disagree with earlier researchers who have claimed stress on the penult') and Clynes & Deterding 2011: 265, who identify the pattern as a phrase-final rise-fall that skips a schwa penult, not word stress.

ev.cite: Winstedt, R.O. 1913. Malay Grammar. Oxford: Clarendon Press (1st edition; StressTyp2 cites the 1927 2nd edition). Sec. 14 'Accent', pp. 30-31 (archive.org malaygrammar00winsrich, PDF leaves 34-35)
ev.text: § 14. Accent. The need to discuss accent tends to give an exaggerated idea of its importance in Malay. It is necessary to bear in mind that there is no strong accent on any syllable in a Malay word; that words like pĕrkataan, pĕrbuatan, aluran, kĕdĕngaran, di-katakan, for example, are pronounced practically with the same stress on every syllable. 776.dq: there are no phenomena in spoken Malay corresponding to what phonologists call stress, and that the whole notion of stress is completely irrelevant in the description of Malay ... We therefore disagree with earlier researchers who have claimed stress on the penult.
776.dloc: Sec. 10 'Conclusion' (online HTML edition of the journal, unpaginated; Internet Archive text capture)
776.prule: No word stress. Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008 (instrumental: duration and F0 of 111 words produced in citation form by two native speakers, then annotated connected speech) conclude that 'there are no phenomena in spoken Malay corresponding to what phonologists call stress'; the apparent penultimate prominence of a word said on its own is the onset rise plus final cadence of a one-word phrase, and where the penult has a central vowel (schwa) the pitch peak is delayed to the final syllable (secs. 9-10). Clynes & Deterding 2011: 265 (Standard Malay of Brunei) likewise find no inherent lexical stress: a rise-fall pitch movement across the penultimate and final syllables of a phrase 'can create an impression of penultimate word stress', and where the penult has /ə/ the movement is usually confined to the phrase-final syllable. The earlier rule (Winstedt 1913 sec. 14: accent ordinarily on the penult, on the last syllable when the penult is an open ĕ syllable; 'no strong accent on any syllable in a Malay word') is carried under the dissenting descriptions as superseded.
776.srule: Not applicable: the descriptions followed find no word stress (Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008 sec. 10: Malay 'has no stress or tone or any other intermediate level of prosodic organisation'; Clynes & Deterding 2011: 265), so no secondary stress is described. The superseded description, Winstedt 1913 sec. 14 'Accent', pp. 30-32, mentions none either ('no strong accent on any syllable in a Malay word').
776.quote: [Zuraidah Mohd Don, Knowles & Yong 2008, sec. 10 'Conclusion'] The first conclusion to be drawn is that there are no phenomena in spoken Malay corresponding to what phonologists call stress, and that the whole notion of stress is completely irrelevant in the description of Malay. The pitch may go up and down, loudness and tempo may increase or decrease, and on occasion the effect may be superficially similar to that produced by stress in a language like English; but these phenomena are all accounted for independently of stress. ... We therefore disagree with earlier researchers who have claim…
776.loc: Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008: Sec. 10 'Conclusion' (online HTML edition of the journal, unpaginated; Internet Archive text capture); Clynes & Deterding 2011: 'Stress and intonation', p. 265
776.idn: Standard Malay of Peninsular Malaysia ('schwa-variety Standard Malay', Clynes & Deterding 2011: 265); data: 111 citation-form words from two female native speakers plus annotated connected speech (Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008). Second description: Standard Malay of Brunei. Superseded: Winstedt 1913 (Malay Peninsula).

tn.quote: The first conclusion to be drawn is that there are no phenomena in spoken Malay corresponding to what phonologists call stress, and that the whole notion of stress is completely irrelevant in the description of Malay. … Malay has a reputation as a “simple” language, whatever that means. … One of its more interesting properties is that it has no stress or tone or any other intermediate level of prosodic organisation. This makes Malay an ideal language to work on for the investigation of prosodic structure.
tn.cite: Zuraidah Mohd Don, Gerry Knowles & Janet Yong. 2008. How words can be misleading: A study of syllable timing and 'stress' in Malay. The Linguistics Journal 3(2) (August 2008). (live URL dead)
tn.locator: Section 10 'Conclusion', first paragraph and sixth (penultimate) paragraph beginning 'Malay has a reputation as a "simple" language' (HTML article, no page numbers)
tn.note: No lexical tone and no word stress: F0 study of 111 words (two speakers) plus read phrases finds only a phrase-onset rise to a penult peak and a final falling cadence, i.e. utterance-level prosody.

776.sec_cite: Winstedt, R.O. 1913. Malay Grammar, sec. 14 'Accent', pp. 30-31 (superseded description)
776.cfw: Three modern instrumental studies (Zuraidah Mohd Don, Knowles & Yong 2008; Clynes & Deterding 2011; Wan Aslynn 2012) find no lexical word stress in Standard Malay, only a phrase-final rise-fall that sounds like penultimate stress and moves to the last syllable when the penult is schwa, so the penultimate rule of Winstedt 1913, who himself wrote that no syllable carries a strong accent, describes that phrase-level pattern rather than word stress.

777.dq: The last syllable of a word consisting of two or more syllables does not take the accent.
777.dloc: Vol. I, Part First, ch. V 'The Accent', §§28-31, pp. 27-28 (archive.org item grammarofarabicl01caspuoft, pp. 45-46)
777.heavy: 'long by nature' = an open syllable containing a long vowel (§29) and 'long by position' = a shut (closed) syllable (§30); diphthongs ei/au count as long (ḳu-béi-la, bil-láu-run). Final syllables count only in pausal forms whose (then superheavy CVVC/CVCC) last syllable keeps its accent (§28a).
777.dflt: initial ('thrown as far back as possible': ká-ta-ba-tā, ḳá-ṣa-ba-tu-hu-mā)
777.prule: The accent never falls on the last syllable of a polysyllable (except pausal forms like kā-ti-bât, ya-ḳûl, fi-rínd, which keep the accent of the full form). The penult is accented if long by nature (long vowel) or by position (closed). If the penult is short, the antepenult is accented when the word has at most three syllables or when the antepenult is long by nature or position; otherwise 'the accent is thrown as far back as possible' (ká-ta-ba-tā, más-'a-la-tu-hā, ḳá-ṣa-ba-tu-hu-mā).
777.srule: Not mentioned in Wright 1896, vol. I, ch. V 'The Accent' secs 28-31, pp. 27-28 (whole chapter read; it places one accent per word and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic accents).

morph.elicq: Wright gives the accent rules as normative statements with syllabified citation forms and no statement of how they were observed; the only pointer to evidence is §31 Rem. (vol. 777.cfw: Wright 1896, Socin 1885, Brame 1970, McCarthy 1979, Thelwall and Sa'adeddin 1990, Halpern 2009 and Watson 2011 all describe Standard Arabic stress as weight-sensitive (a final superheavy syllable, else the heavy penult, else the antepenult), and the only disagreement, which Watson 2011 records as unresolved, is whether stress in words whose penult and antepenult are both light stops at the antepenult (Brame 1970, Halpern 2009) or retracts to the first syllable (Wright 1896, Socin 1885, McCarthy 1979). One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Wright 1896.

778.dq: Stress falls on the second syllable of a word, and on monosyllables. (Hayes 1995:267 on Dakota incl. Stoney, citing Shaw 1985a,b); 'primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable in longer words' (Wesley & Telfer 2022:3 n.3).
778.dloc: Shaw 1985:1 (StressTyp2 entry); Hayes 1995:267 (d) and footnote 19; Wesley & Telfer 2022:3 n.3
778.heavy: Final syllable only: CVCC (doubly closed) counts as heavy vs CVC light; no phonemic vowel length (Hayes 1995:267 n.19 summarizing Shaw 1985; ST1 note ': doubly closed syllables'). Hayes offers a reanalysis as final-C extrasyllabicity + syllable extrametricality rather than true weight.
778.dflt: penult (under the emerging rule); second syllable under the inherited Dakota rule
778.prule: Two coexisting/competing rules (Shaw 1985): (a) the inherited Dakota rule, stress on the second syllable of the word (monosyllables stressed); (b) an emerging Stoney rule, stress the final syllable if it is heavy (CVCC), otherwise the penult. Shaw frames (b) as an ongoing development; Wesley & Telfer 2022 describe present-day Stoney stress as phonemic with a penultimate tendency in longer words.
778.srule: Morley Stoney: one secondary stress on the second syllable (relic Dakota Stress Rule) beside penultimate primary, e.g. akìda-bí-kta-č 'they will look at it', ī-yì-ktō-ktō-ðá-bi-č 'we (pl) are sawing' (Shaw 1985a:7, 14 as reported in Rhyasen Erdman 1997:68-69, 73; Shaw 1985a:15 n. notes words over five syllables with more than one secondary; RE disputes the DSR account). Alexis Stoney (RE 1997 (20) p.63, (45) p.76, own fieldwork): secondary on every other syllable right-to-left from the primary; all long vowels and monosyllabic roots stressed.

[Hayes 1995:267] (d) Dakota (Siouan, Great Plains; Chambers 1978; Shaw 1985a, 1985b). Stress falls on the second syllable of a word, and on monosyllables. This suggests that a single even iamb is assigned at the left edge of a word. ... 19. Shaw's detailed analysis of the Stoney dialect also includes a second stress rule, claimed to be sensitive to syllable…
778.loc: Shaw 1985:1 (StressTyp2 entry); Hayes 1995:267 (d) and footnote 19; Wesley & Telfer 2022:3 n.3
778.idn: 'the Stoney dialect' [of Dakota] (Hayes 1995 n.19 summarizing Shaw 1985; Hayes's (d) sentence itself is about Dakota as a whole); 'the southern dialect of Stoney, also known as Stoney Nakoda' incl. Mînî Thnî (Morley) (Wesley & Telfer 2022); 'Alexis Stoney' (Rhyasen Erdman 1997) (a named variety of the language)…
778.exq_: Stress is phonemic in Stoney, and primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable in longer words. (Wesley & Telfer 2022:3 n.3) ... [gendered enclitics] typically do not receive stress or interact with the prosodic system at all (they appear to be largely extrametrical). (p.4)

secx.primary_revised_quote: the concatenation of the perfective and declarative morphemes does not create a superheavy syllable, as defined by Shaw (1985a). If the final syllable is not a superheavy syllable in perfective structures then it is not syllable structure which is marked for stress. The final syllable in perfective structures is stressed because the perfective morpheme, itself, is inherently marked for stress.

st.weight_quote: Since there is no phonemic vowel length in Dakota, and the claimed quantity distinction is one of final CVC vs. CVCC, there is an alternative: assume final C in CVCC to be temporarily extrasyllabic, as in Arabic (§5.2.1), and let penultimate stress be assigned by syllable extrametricality and End Rule Right. The stray consonant would block extrametricality, so that final CVCC would attract stress.

779.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (stem or derived alike); if the penult has schwa and the final syllable a full vowel, stress on the final syllable; if both syllables of a disyllable have schwa, regular penult stress. morph.rootq: Coolsma 1904 sec. 8 p. 8: 'Regel is bij het spreken, dat de voorlaatste lettergreep van het woord den klemtoon krijgt, om het even of het een stamwoord dan wel een afgeleid woord geldt.' [The rule in speaking is that the penultimate syllable of the WORD gets the stress, no matter whether it is a root word or a derived word.] BUT two sub-rules refer to the root: 'Tweelettergrepige woorden, met een toonlooze e in beide lettergrepen, z. a. bĕnĕr, lĕrĕs en sĕdĕk, krijgen den klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep ... en als zulk een woord een achtervoegsel krijgt, zoo verspringt de klemtoon in den regel op regelmatige wijze naar de laatste lettergreep van het stamwoord'…
morph.elicq: Coolsma 1904 sec. 8 p. 8-9 gives no method; the description is impressionistic and framed in terms of ordinary speaking and reading aloud: 'De Soendaneezen zijn gewoon langzaam en bedaard te spreken, op een eigenaardigen toon (lagoe), die zangerig en gerekt klinkt ... Regel is bij het spreken, dat de voorlaatste lettergreep van het woord den klemtoon krijgt' and, on enclisis of monosyllables, 'zoo beschouwt men het in het spreken of lezen als tot dat voorafgaande woord te behooren'; it also covers sentence-level prosody ('Het einde van een zin wordt doorgaans zeer gerekt en zangerig uitgesproken, en de voorlaatste lettergreep van den zin krijgt meestal een bijzonderen nadruk'), i.e.…
morph.stmt: Hardjadibrata 1985 sec. 2.2 p. 7: 'The derivation of words in Sundanese is by affixation, reduplication and compounding. The most predominant word formation made is affixation' -- with a mixed profile: voice (AV homorganic nasal N-/nga-, PV di-/ka-), benefactive pang-, verbalising di-/ba-/pa-/si-/ti- and several nominalisers (ka-, pa-, pang-, pi-) are prefixes, the plural/agreement markers -ar-/-um-/-in- are infixes, while causative/applicative -keun, applicative/iterative -an, nominalising -an/-eun, 3rd-person -eun and possessive/definite -na are suffixes, and many nominalisations are circumfixal (ka-...-an, pa-...-an, pi-...-eun); Kurniawan 2013 p. 22 adds 'There is neither case nor…

But apart from this general and fixed stress, he makes use of some little words whose sole purpose is to lay a certain emphasis.…
secx.primary_revised_quote: stress appeared to be noncontrastive and apparently nonphonemic. ... When any of the informants pronounced words in isolation, however, the words were almost invariably pronounced with level stress and level intonation. ... 779.cfw: Coolsma 1904 and Clynes 1995 (after Robins 1953) put stress on the penult, moving to the final syllable when the penult vowel is schwa, but Van Syoc 1959 found no lexical stress at all in his three speakers and Kaufman and Himmelmann 2024 group Sundanese with the stressless languages of Java, so whether Sundanese has word stress at all is still an open question.

780.dq: Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of words up to six syllables in length. (section 3 is headed 'PHONOLOGICAL WORD PATTERNS'; p. 12 separately: 'on the stressed syllable of the last word of the sentence a rise occurs', i.e. sentence intonation docks on word stress)
780.dloc: p. 9, section 3.1 'Stress'; supporting examples p. 6 [i'təwərə] 'I give' and p. 3 ['sunkənun] 'mosquito'; p. 10 begins section 4 (Syllable Patterns), so 3.1 is the complete stress treatment
780.heavy: A penult with a full (non-schwa) vowel holds stress; a penult whose vowel is /ə/ rejects stress to the antepenult (if one exists). Light = /ə/ nucleus only; no role for vowel length or codas (codas are nasals only, p. 10, and play no part in the rule).
780.dflt: antepenult (shift applies whenever the penult is /ə/, regardless of the antepenult's vowel: p. 6 [i'təwərə]); penult in disyllables
780.prule: Penultimate stress; if the penult vowel is /ə/, stress shifts to the antepenult (if one exists), whatever the antepenult's own vowel; disyllables keep penult stress even on /ə/.
780.srule: None described: the word formula '(S) (S) (S) (S) 'S (S)' and the pattern tables ('S, 'SS, S'SS, SS'SS, SSS'SS, SSSS'SS; /ə/-penult words 'SSS... SSS'SSS) mark one stressed syllable per word of up to six syllables; the paper (section 3.1 is its whole stress treatment) says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.
780.quote: 3.1. STRESS Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of words up to six syllables in length. In cases when the penultimate syllable has a /ə/ vowel, the stress is shifted to the ante-penultimate syllable if such a syllable exists. Since an ante-penultimate syllable cannot exist in two syllable words, stress occurs on the penultimate syllable even though it is a /ə/. The basic patterns may be summarized as follows: (S) (S) (S) (S) 'S (S) This formula implies the following word patterns: 'S 'SS S'SS SS'SS SSS'SS SSSS'SS In words of three or more syllables with /ə/ in the penultimate syllable, …

In cases when the penultimate syllable has a /ə/ vowel, the stress is shifted to the ante-penultimate syllable if such a syllable exists. Since an ante-penultimate syllable cannot exist in two syllable words, stress occurs on the penultimate syllable even though it is a /ə/." (Collier & Collier 1986:9, §3.1). The rule is stated over the word with no reference to root or affix; the illustrating forms include an inflected verb [i'təwərə] /itəwərə/ 'I give' (p.6), and Collier & Gregerson 1985:163 rule (ii) 'e is deleted following a stressed syllable and a nasal' marks stress on a suffix vowel: meko-y-án(e)-re…

morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing on the verb: "the nominal suffixes, S and O, typically follow the ROOT in the order indicated" (schema ROOT - S - O - ASP, with Mode/Tense placement varying; Collier & Gregerson 1985 §0.3 p.157); negation is "ROOT + -i + pai" with pai "postposed to the verb root" (§5 p.171); NP relations are marked by postposed re 'from' / te GOAL-Object (§3.2); the only pre-verbal elements are free words (adverb, auxiliary verb: "VP = ADV - AUXV - V - NEG", §0.2). No prefix of any kind appears in the source; 0 prefix morphs in 80 tokens.

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Tahitian: primary stress on the left-most heavy syllable, else on the final syllable; no secondary stress". The source gives: Tryon 1976:6 / Hayes 1980: stress the leftmost (first) long vowel or vowel cluster in the word; if the word has only short vowels, stress the penult. (Bickmore 1995, as reported by Walker 1997 fn.10, confines primary stress to the last three syllables.) — StressTyp2 F/L prose 'the left-most heavy syllable, else on the final syllable' matches Tryon's leftmost-heavy clause but states the default as final where Tryon/Hayes say penult; StressTyp2's own ST1 remark reconciles this via right-edge extrametricality…

ev.text: An example is Tahitian, as discussed in Tyron (1976), Vergnaud and Halle (1978). The stress pattern of this language is as follows: (3) a. Stress the leftmost long vowel or vowel cluster. b. Otherwise stress the penult. As Tyron states that vowel clusters in Tahitian are tautosyllabic, this stress pattern can be expressed very simply in the following way: (4) a. On the [+syl] projection, form a right dominant, unbounded foot, labeling dominant nodes as strong iff they branch. b. Form a left dominant word tree. Some examples are: ... tamaaroa "boy" ... pahii "ship" ... ?ohipa "work" ... fare "house" ... The crucial cases here are (5)e and f. Because these words contain no long vowels, they a…

Form a left dominant word tree.'; Walker 1997 fn.10: 'limited to a…
781.dloc: Tryon, D. T. (1970). Conversational Tahitian. Canberra: Australian National University Press, sec. 8 'Stress', rules (ii)-(iii), p.6 (p.20 of the ANU open copy, hdl 1885/114918); Hayes 1980, p.176, rule (4)b; Walker 1997 ROA-172, fn.10.
781.heavy: a long vowel or a (tautosyllabic) vowel cluster / 'sequence of vowels' (Tryon via StressTyp2; Hayes 'long vowel or vowel cluster'); ST1 note: = long vowels. No closed syllables in Tahitian, so coda weight is moot.
781.prule: Tryon 1970:5-6 (StressTyp2's 'Tryon 1976:6') / Hayes 1980: stress the leftmost (first) long vowel or vowel cluster in the word (within a cluster, its first vowel); if the word has only short vowels, stress the penult; in compounds each part takes its own stress, and causative verbs carry two primary stresses, one on the prefix fa'a-/ha'a- and one on the verb stem (Tryon 1970:41 fn.). Tryon adds that primary stress 'is not nearly so heavy as in English in many words, and at times it appears that no particular syllable bears the primary stress'. (Bickmore 1995, as reported by Walker 1997 fn.10, confines primary stress to the last three syllables; not opened.)
781.srule: Only for complex words: in compounds 'each part of the compound takes its own stress' (Tryon 1970 sec. 8 rule iv: pua'a-niho, pua'a-horo-fenua), and causative fa'a-/ha'a- verbs have 'two primary stresses, one on the prefix and one on the verb stem' (sec. 49 fn., p.41). No secondary or rhythmic stress is described for simple words in Tryon 1970 sec. 8 or Hayes 1980 pp.175-177.
781.quote: An example is Tahitian, as discussed in Tyron (1976), Vergnaud and Halle (1978). The stress pattern of this language is as follows: (3) a. Stress the leftmost long vowel or vowel cluster. b. Otherwise stress the penult. As Tyron states that vowel clusters in Tahitian are tautosyllabic, this stress pattern can be expressed very simply in the following way: (4) a. On the [+syl] projection, form a right dominant, unbounded foot, labeling dominant nodes as strong iff they branch. b. Form a left dominant word tree. morph.rootq: Tryon 1970 §8 pp.5-6 gives purely phonological rules: '(i) In words containing either a sequence of different vowels or a long vowel, the stress falls on the first vowel of the sequence, or on the long vowel. (ii) With words containing two such sequences ... the stress falls on the first of the sequences in the word. (iii) With words not containing long vowels or sequences of vowels, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. (iv) With compound words, usually polysyllabic, each part of the compound takes its own stress.' The only morphological reference is the footnote to §49 (p.41, causative): 'With causative verbs, there are two primary stresses, one on the prefix and one on the verb…
morph.elicq: Tryon 1970 §8 p.5-6: 'In Tahitian, the primary stress is not nearly so heavy as in English in many words, and at times it appears that no particular syllable bears the primary stress. However, there are four stress rules which are in evidence:' — followed only by lists of isolated citation words (tiare 'flower', fare 'house', ta'ata 'person', pua'a-horo-fenua 'horse'); no method, frame, text or measurement is mentioned. The Introduction (p.xiv) says only that the book rests on two field stays in Tahiti with 'my principal informant and guide, Mr François Taumihau Peu, of Papeete'.
morph.stmt: Tahitian is overwhelmingly analytic: TAM ('ua, 'e, te…nei/ra, i…na), articles (te, te hō'e), plural (mau), case relators (i, 'ia, 'e, 'o), negators ('aita etc.), the polar-question particle (anei) and directionals are free particles, mostly preposed to the lexical head ('No plural sign is added to the noun itself', Tryon §11); the only bound morphology the grammar describes is the causative PREFIXES fa'a-/ha'a-/tā- ('The prefixes used to form the causative are fa'a- or ha'a-', §49) versus the post-root nominaliser -ra'a ('the nominalising suffix -ra'a converts verbs into nouns, almost without exception', §46c) and passive hia/-a ('placing hia after the verb stem', §47), plus partial/full…

morph.rootq: Besold 2012 A.3.5.1 pp.113-114: 'The general stress pattern in SCLs is commonly observed in AALs (Dixon, 2002a:557). Stress falls on the first syllable in disyllabic words and no example is found in the source material that shows stress on the final syllable in a disyllabic word. ... In words with three syllables or more, primary stress falls on the first or second syllable. Where stress is marked on a second syllable in a polysyllabic word, a long vowel in that stressed syllable is in some cases indicated.' The statement is by syllable count within the word; root/stem and suffixes are not mentioned (all cited examples are unsuffixed nouns, mostly from the Dhurga/Djirringanj wordlists).
morph.elicq: Besold 2012 A.3.5 p.112: 'Information on stress assignment is found in the transcriptions of some of the early collectors. Mathews and Howitt marked many words in their wordlists for stress with an apostrophe at the end of the stressed syllable, i.e. mabara 'eye' shows the stress assigned on the first syllable in <mab'-o-ra> (U-M.1.1) and <ma'bra> (DJ-AH.1.3). Later, and in contrast, Tindale marked stress at the beginning of a stressed syllable as in the same word <'mabara> (WL-T.75).'…
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing/encliticising: 'The noun structure in all SCLs is Root-(derivation)-(inflections)' (A.4 p.156); 'Verbs and nouns are distinguished by the type of suffixing they can take' (A.6.1 p.284); verb inflection is described 'from the end of the word inwards towards the word stem' with 'Subject and object... marked in that order in verb-final position' as bound pronouns/enclitics (A.5 pp.231-232); no prefix or proclitic of any kind is described anywhere in the grammar, and the word 'prefix' does not occur in chs A.3-A.7.

contra.head: A 19th-century grammar places the accent on the root, or on the last member of a compound
contra.detail: Jäschke's grammar (1883 2nd ed.; the 1954 Ungar edition is its reprint) makes an impressionistic statement, with no method stated, about words made of a nominal or verbal root plus postposed monosyllabic 'terminations' (case particles etc.) and about compounds: 'The accent is, in such cases, most naturally given to the root, or, in compounds, generally to the latter part of the composition, as: mig,eye', mig-gi,of the eye'; lag,hand', lag-šub(s),hand-covering, glove'.' (p. 13, §9 ¶4). He then ties vowel quantity to accent for Western Tibetan and says Central Tibetan (the group that includes Lhasa) shortens even accented vowels: 'Equally natural is, in W.T., the quantity of the vowels: accen…

tn.quote: Tone (pitch) is a distinctive feature of Lhasa Tibetan. Each single or geminate (long) vowel has a particular tone in each syllable. ... Four tonal phonemes are differentiated in this manual: (1) high tone, which is indicated by a line above the vowel or vowels, e.g., tā; (2) low tone, which is indicated by a line below the vowel or vowels, e.g., ta̱; (3) falling tone, which is indicated by an oblique line above the second of geminate vowels, e.g., tāà, ta̱à; and (4) mid tone, which is not marked at all, e.g., so̱mo. The mid tone never occurs in the initial stressed position.
tn.cite: Goldstein, Melvyn C. & Nawang Nornang (1978). Modern Spoken Tibetan: Lhasa Dialect. 2nd ed., ed. H.K. Kuloy. Kathmandu: Ratna Pustak Bhandar (Bibliotheca Himalayica). [1st ed. 1970, Seattle: University of Washington Press.]
tn.note: Four tonal phonemes (high, low, falling, mid) on each syllable; falling written only on long (geminate) vowels; mid unmarked, never in initial stressed position. Word stress by vowel length also.

783.cfw: Goldstein and Nornang 1978 give a hedged note that the longer syllable of a Lhasa Tibetan disyllable tends to carry stress and Meredith 1990 describes a weight- and tone-sensitive stress within the first two syllables, but the one instrumental study, Lim 2018, finds no word stress at all, and Tournadre and Suzuki 2023 treat stress as at most a secondary feature under a pitch system with an initial strong-weak pattern, so authoritative sources disagree on whether Lhasa Tibetan has word stress and, if so, where it falls. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Goldstein 1978.

784.dq: Primary stress falls on the penult or antepenult of polysyllabic bases ... Secondary stress may occur on words of four or more syllables, and falls on the second syllable preceding the primary stress. Stress in Tiruray is noncontrastive and nonphonemic
784.dloc: p. 7 section 'Stress' and p. 8 first sentence; with p. 7 'Syllable patterning' and p. 6 vowel entry for plain e (the central vowel, distinct from e-acute) giving the 'shortened allophone'
784.heavy: No heavy/light or long/short syllable classes are defined; syllables are CV and CVC only and there is no vowel-length contrast. The only stated conditioning is negative: when the vowels of the penult/antepenult are 'shortened', stress goes to the ultima. Per the same key the vowel with a 'shortened allophone' is plain e (high close, mid [central], unrounded vocoid, the schwa-like sixth vowel, printed without the acute that marks front e-acute), shortened in open syllables and before a place-assimilating nasal after glottal stop; this e never occurs word-finally, so the ultima always has a full vowel. Closed syllables are not said to attract stress (apart from the reduplication double-stress remark).
784.dflt: penult or antepenult (source does not say which)
784.prule: Primary stress on the penult or antepenult of polysyllabic bases (the choice between the two is not conditioned in the text and no examples are given); on the ultima when the vowels of the penult/antepenult are shortened (reduced central e); when reduplication yields two identical closed syllables in a base, both carry primary stress; stress is 'noncontrastive and nonphonemic' and unmarked in the lexicon.
784.srule: Optional secondary stress in words of four or more syllables, on the second syllable preceding the primary stress (one secondary stated; no iteration, weight condition or examples given).

785.dq: I. De klemtoon valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep. a. bij tweelettergrepige woorden van Tobel. oorsprong. ... c. Bij alle woorden die verbonden zijn met een tweelettergrepig achtervoegsel. Het achtervoegsel trekt dan den klemtoon tot zich op zijn voorlaatsten lettergreep.

785.heavy: A final syllable containing a diphthong (tweeklank) or a long contracted vowel ('langen saamgetrokken klank', e.g. damā) attracts stress to the ultima; Hueting motivates this historically as two vowels of which the first was stressed. Closed syllables play no role (not mentioned; Tobelo syllables are open).

Fleming & Dennis 1977:127 (quoted verbatim in Garrett ROA-1031 sec.3.3): 'in a majority of cases, stress occurs on the final syllable of consonant-final words [phesmás 'skunk'] and the penultimate syllable of vowel-final words [phésme 'skunk'] ... However, stress may also occur on the final syllable of vowel final words [ʔisí 'water', chiyó 'dog'] and, less frequently, on the penultimate syllable of consonant-final words.' Both statements are framed on the word and its final segment; neither mentions root, stem or affixes.
morph.elicq: No statement of evidence type in the accessible material: the dictionary's rule (p.57) is given as an orthographic accent convention without saying how stress was determined, and the verbatim Fleming & Dennis 1977:127 passage (via Garrett) illustrates the rule with isolated citation forms (phesmás/phésme 'skunk', ʔisí 'water', chiyó 'dog') but does not say whether stress was observed in isolation, frames or texts; the IJAL primary itself was not reachable (paywall).
morph.stmt: Mixed, verb-prefixing for tense/mood and suffixing for person: 'Hay dos clases de verbos las cuales se distinguen por la serie de afijos que utilizan' (Dennis & Dennis 1983:63), 'Las clases se distinguen por los sufijos de los verbos' (p.v) -- past ti-/tje- and future m-/n- are prefixes, subject person-number is suffixal (-a, -n, -s, -ucj, -pj) except 3pl present ja-, with stem-internal -y- infixation; nouns take possessive prefixes ('indicada dicha forma por un prefijo nasal', p.vi) and plural suffixes -tjacj/-pan; object pronouns, reflexive markers, negation ma and irrealis ca are separate preverbal words, and imperfective =cha is enclitic (Haurholm-Larsen 2014).

787.dq: There are three degrees of stress: unstress (unmarked), word stress (ˊ) and phrase stress (ˋ). ... Word stress is replaced by stronger stress on the last word of a phrase: /bale/ [bàlɛ] the house /bale waŋko?/ [bálɛ wàŋkɔ?] the big house
787.heavy: Sneddon never uses the term 'heavy'. Stated stress-relevant properties of nuclei: (a) a 'long vocoid, which is interpreted as two phonemic syllable nuclei, takes stress if it is in the last or second-last phonetic syllable in the word' (last wins if both are long); (b) a penultimate /ə/ loses stress to the final syllable only if the final nucleus is a vowel other than /ə/ AND 'it is separated from the penultimate syllable by just one consonant' (words of 2-3 syllables, or 4+ with a schwa antepenult); in 4+ syllable words with a full-vowel antepenult the antepenult takes stress instead; where these conditions fail (schwa penult followed by a consonant cluster, /təmpok/ [tə́mpɔk], /kaanəŋku/ [ka:nə́ŋku], or all-schwa words, /rəpət/ [rə́pət], /wəʔŋəl/) 'Penultimate schwa takes stress'. So the number of consonants after a schwa penult (open vs closed schwa syllable) matters by the stated rule, but closed syllables with full vowels play no stated role; (c) a lower vowel immediately preceding the penultimate vowel takes stress; (d) across a glottal stop, a preceding vowel identical to or lower than the penultimate vowel takes stress. Effective scale: long vocoid (VV) > full vowel (lower > higher) > /ə/ (closed > open).
787.prule: Regular word stress: penultimate syllable, except (a) a long vocoid in the last or second-last phonetic syllable takes stress (last wins if both long); (b) penultimate /ə/: stress goes to the final syllable (non-schwa nucleus, exactly one intervening consonant, 2-3 syllable words or 4+ with schwa antepenult) or to the antepenult (4+ syllables with non-schwa antepenult); otherwise (schwa + cluster, all-schwa words) the schwa penult keeps stress; (c) a lower vowel immediately preceding the penultimate vowel takes stress; (d) across glottal stop, a preceding identical or lower vowel takes stress. Irregular (morphological) stress with certain affixes/clitics.

morph.elicq: The stress section gives no statement of how stress was determined; evidence shown is isolated words with phonetic transcription ("/wale/ [wále] house", "/tikoo/ [tikó:] throat") plus two- and three-word phrases for phrase stress: "Word stress is replaced by stronger stress on the last word of a phrase: /bale/ [bálɛ] the house, /bale waŋkoʔ/ ... the big house, /bale waŋkoʔ rua/ ... the two big houses" (p.12); "No instances of minimal stress contrast have been recorded but contrast in terms of CVCV structure does occur" (p.9). 788.heavy: long vowel = two morae (pēpē [ˌpeːˈpeː] takes final stress); no codas exist (all syllables open), so CVC weight never arises; VV sequences of unlike vowels likewise count two morae
788.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate mora of the phonological word ('moraic trochee at right edge', White & Garellek AFLA18 slides after Churchward 1953/Feldman 1978): i.e. final syllable if it contains a long vowel (bimoraic), otherwise the penultimate syllable/vowel; a long vowel whose second half is the penultimate mora is broken into two syllables with stress on the second (maama [ma.ˈa.ma]).
788.srule: Secondary stresses occur but their placement is 'much less apparent' than primary stress: reported as alternating syllables subject to morpheme boundaries (Feldman 1978: 'every second vowel from the end of each morpheme', as quoted by Zuraw, O'Flynn & Ward 2019) or as unpredictable, especially in loans; the authors' summary is 'Secondary stress assignment depends on morphology (Feldman 1978) and can be variable for loanwords'. In their 4-mora test words (CVCV'CV-ni, e.g. nenenuni [ne.ne.'nu.ni]; pēpē [pe:'pe:]) it falls on the leftmost vowel/mora.

789.dq: Het is echter duidelijk te hooren, dat de klemtoon in het Tt. valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep van het woord, onverschillig of het een stamwoord is van twee, drie of meer lettergrepen, of wel een afgeleid woord ... (p. 41)
789.dloc: Hoofdstuk I (Klankstelsel), section 'De klemtoon', pp. 41-42 (Delpher KB scan MMSFKB02:000036333, scan pages 00047-00048)
789.heavy: A final syllable that is closed ('gesloten') AND has a, e or o as its vowel attracts stress, but only when the penult has ë (schwa); a prenasalised or preglottalised onset of the final syllable (i.e. nasal/glottal effectively closing the schwa penult) usually keeps stress on the penult. Schwa itself is stressable (ë́nëp, kë́lës). No vowel length contrast (length is conditioned by stress, p. 11).
789.prule: Stress (klemtoon, realised mainly as pitch rise) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, whether root or derived, regardless of length; only when the penult has ë and the final syllable is closed with vowel a/e/o does stress 'dikwerf' (often) fall on the final syllable, and even then 'gewoonlijk' (usually) stays on the penult if the final syllable begins with a prenasalised or preglottalised consonant. 'Vaste regels hieromtrent te geven is ons nog niet mogelijk.'
789.srule: Not mentioned in Adriani & Adriani-Gunning 1908, Hoofdstuk I 'De klemtoon', pp. 41-42 (whole section read: one word stress and its position; no secondary or rhythmic stress). Also not mentioned in Ticoalu et al. 1984 sec. 1.6.1 (p. 13) or Robot, Kalangi & Imbang 2019; Kembuan et al. 1988 Fonologi Bahasa Tontemboan not obtained.

790.dq: Tübatulabal employs a free word-stress which expresses no systematic meaning ... Thus the word, in Tübatulabal, is a phonetic entity delimited by the position of the main stress. Conjunctive particles which follow the main stress are either atonic or accented independently
790.dloc: §4 'Stress and the syllable', pp. 75-79 (main stress p. 75; alternation of stress pp. 76-77; fixed stress pp. 78-79; closed syllables without mora value p. 79 §6.i)
790.heavy: Mora count of vowels only: long (and long rearticulated) vowel = two morae, short vowel = one mora; consonants have no mora value (closed syllables explicitly listed under 'Variations of Syllabic Length Which Have No Mora Value', p.79), except the organic glottal stop, which counts one mora.
790.dflt: Main stress final; alternate stresses on every second vowel counting leftward from it (final, antepenultimate...).
790.prule: Main stress on the final vowel of the word: the final vowel of the stem, or, if suffixes are appended, the final vowel of the last suffix (quantity-insensitive; 'with very few exceptions'). Conjunctive particles (enclitics) after the main stress are atonic or independently accented and lie outside the stress word.
790.srule: Alternate stresses on every second mora counting right-to-left from the final main stress (short V = 1 mora, long V = 2; consonants moraless except the organic glottal stop = 1 mora); when the count lands on the second mora of a long vowel the stress falls on that long vowel (third mora back), so a long vowel before short+stressed is itself stressed. Two identical short vowels split by a glottal stop within one morpheme count as one unit; in the few fixed-stress elements the fixed vowel restarts the count. Voegelin: main stress 'is not acoustically more prominent than other stressed vowels'.
790.quote: Tübatulabal employs a free word-stress which expresses no systematic meaning: words are never distinguished by a difference in accentuation. ... Alternation of stress in general is oriented from the main stress, which is not acoustically more prominent than other stressed vowels, but merely serves as a convenient point of departure in describing the rhythmical pattern. 1. The Main Stress. With very few exceptions (cf. 3, 4, below), the main stress falls on the final vowel of the stem; or if suffixes are appended, on the final vowel of the last suffix. ... 2.
