792.heavy: heavy = syllable containing a long vowel and/or a coda consonant ([C0VC] or [C0V:C0]); light = [C0V]; onsets irrelevant (p.43). In clash resolution long-vowel stress outranks closed-syllable stress (p.64).
792.dflt: peninitial (head of [LL] iamb, with iambic lengthening: suyu-ka [suyú:ka], wasa-ratikna [wasá:ratikna]); bare LL nouns oscillate between initial and final ([áwa] ~ [awá:])
792.prule: An initial iambic foot ([H], [LL] or [LH]) is built at the left edge of the stem and its head (rightmost syllable) is stressed: initial syllable if heavy, otherwise the second syllable. For canonical adjectives this is the root-final syllable without exception (p.57); for canonical verbs it holds for all consonant-themed forms (p.58), but consonant-final 0-class stems with vowel-initial suffixes resyllabify so the iamb head falls outside the root on the suffix-initial vowel (wat-am [watám], pp.58-59), vowel-themed roots likewise with iambic lengthening of that vowel (yaw-arang [yawá:rang], p.59), and with PROX -i the (C)VCV word obligatorily retracts to initial stress (trochaic: wat-i [wáti], p.59). All long vowels are stressed; one of the first three syllables is stressed; word-final syllables generally unstressed; inflectional suffixes normally unstressed (p.56 ex.49). Bare bisyllabic LL/LH nouns waver between trochaic (initial) and iambic (final) stress because nouns avoid word-final stress; suffixed nouns are uniformly iambic (pp.60-62). LLHL tiwiliski shows a 'double upbeat' to the non-final heavy third syllable (p.64).
792.srule: Green does not rank primary against secondary: 'strong stress', generally one per word, two or more in morphologically complex words (p.56). Additional stresses: every underlying long vowel is stressed, so AUD -î and IMPER22NEG -nînah add a stress after the root stress (clash tolerated; the rightmost generally sounds more prominent, p.60); oversized noun stems parse iteratively into iambs from the left with the final syllable ignored, giving two stresses in long words (sîkakaira [sí:kakàyra], wangkaramah [wàŋkará:mah], kâsiramah [ká:sirá:mah]; 'from three forms only'), long-vowel stress stronger than closed-syllable stress, one stress deleted in initial HH (pp.63-64); no iteration into inflectional or construct suffixes (pp.58, 65); N+N/N+A compounds stress each root (p.68).

793.caution: The primary description (Goddard 1979:21, 130) was not reached; the rule is carried second-hand by Hayes 1995 (as digested in StressTyp2), Hagstrom 1997 (p. 30 fn. 42) and a Wikipedia article. A reading of the primary is still needed.
793.dq: Stress is generally predictable in Unami. The rightmost nonfinal strong vowel is stressed, or a strong vowel in final position if it is the only one in the word. (Wikipedia carrying Goddard 1979:21); Hayes via StressTyp2: 'Main stress is on the rightmost non-final stress.'
793.dloc: Goddard 1979:21 (strong/weak vowels, stress rule), 130 (stress shift in conjunct endings) as carried; Hayes 1995:211-215 via StressTyp2 entry; Hagstrom 1997 (ROA-219), p. 30 fn. 42; Wikipedia wikitext, 'Phonology' > vowels and 'Stress' paragraphs.
793.heavy: 'Strong' vowels: long vowels and (short) vowels before consonant clusters are automatically strong (Hayes: 'CV: and CVC heavy, CV light'); in runs of short-vowel + single C (or Cw) syllables the even-numbered vowels counting from the left are strong (iambic count); a lexical set of breve-marked short /i e o/ behave as long (strong).
793.dflt: All-light words: iambic count from the left makes even-numbered vowels strong; main stress on the rightmost non-final of these (LL disyllable -> final/peninitial; LLL -> second; LLLL -> second (antepenult) since the 4th is final).
793.prule: Main stress falls on the rightmost non-final strong vowel of the word (i.e. the penult if strong, else the antepenult); a word-final strong vowel is stressed only if it is the only strong vowel in the word (so disyllables: initial if strong, else final). Hagstrom paraphrases the same rule as 'the penultimate strong vowel'.
793.srule: All strong vowels other than the main-stressed one plausibly bear secondary stress (Hayes 1995's inference from their resistance to vowel reduction): long vowels, vowels before consonant clusters, and the even-numbered vowels counted left-to-right in runs of short-vowel open syllables (weight-sensitive L->R iambs); none on the final syllable (StressTyp2 coding of the same analysis).

794.cfw: Strong (1914) puts the accent on the first syllable of two-syllable words and the second syllable of longer ones (or the first when a trisyllable contains a diphthong), Kim and Kim (1998) describe predictable penultimate stress with a four-syllable example stressed on the penult, Kim (2002) writes that stress "basically occurs on the second syllable", and Bluhme (1970) found Roro word stress weak with some words confirming Strong's rule and others contradicting it, so the sources agree only that stress is fixed and falls on the first syllable of disyllables and the second of trisyllables, and disagree on longer words and on any weight condition.

795.dq: Therefore, with the exception of a handful of words with a phonemic long vowel in their second syllable, primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word. (p.33); rule (iii): 'Non-branching feet that do not carry primary word stress ... are deleted.' (p.35)
795.dloc: §2.2.4 'Stress placement', pp.33-38 (rule statement p.33, foot rules pp.34-35, caveat p.38); §2.1.4 p.24 (phonemic vs phonetic long vowels)
795.heavy: heavy syllables = 'those containing a phonemic long vowel' (p.33, p.34 rule (i)a); phonetic long vowels derived by /w/-elision do NOT count and do not attract primary stress (p.24, p.37); closed syllables are not mentioned as heavy (e.g. 'garn.gu, 'jam.ba, 'bung.ma pattern with light syllables).
795.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word, except that a phonemic long vowel in the second syllable takes primary stress (ga.'laa 'bone', ga.'rdaa.la 'gidgee tree', Nga.'naa.rra); long vowels occur only in the first or second syllable of a stress domain and 'always receive primary stress irrespective of their position in the word'.
795.srule: Each polysyllabic morpheme is a stress domain; stress falls on the first syllable of each domain and on every alternate syllable after it, the word-final syllable usually unstressed; the leftmost stress is primary, the rest secondary ('ngu.rra.ˌram.ba 'night-time', 'bu.lyu.ˌngu+rna 'little+II', 'da.gu.maj+ˌba.rli 'hit+AGNT', 'jany+ˌbu.lu 'dog+DU'). Monosyllabic suffixes pair with a following monosyllabic suffix or a preceding stray syllable to form a foot, else are unstressed; a heavy syllable (phonemic long vowel) in any morpheme is stressed. Some forms remain unpredictable ('not yet fully understood', p.38).
795.quote: Stress placement in Wambaya is sensitive to morphological structure; each polysyllabic morpheme constitutes a new domain for the placement of stress. Generally stress falls on the first syllable of the stress domain and on each following alternate syllable, except that the final syllable usually does not carry any stress. Stress placement is also sensitive to syllable weight as heavy syllables (i.e. those containing a phonemic long vowel) are always stressed whether they are in the first or second syllable of the stress domain (the only two positional possibilities for long vowels). Therefore…

ev.text: 2.3 STRESS. Stress is assigned as follows: (1) if the first syllable involves a long vowel, then it must receive primary stress; (2) if there is no long vowel in a word, and (a) the word is disyllabic or quadrisyllabic, primary stress goes on the first syllable; (b) the word is trisyllabic or quinquesyllabic, primary stress goes on the second syllable. Secondary stress goes on the syllable next but one after primary stress, except that a final syllable can never bear stress. morph.elicq: §2.3 (pp.20-21) gives the stress rules with isolated citation forms (mu:ba 'stone fish', bada 'dog', gagara 'dilly bag', muŋan / muŋan-da) and no statement of how stress was determined. The corpus itself is described in §1.7 p.14: 'It was possible to record from him [John Tooth] two very short texts, to obtain or check the best part of a thousand lexical items and to elicit on a wide range of grammatical points' - i.e. mostly elicited words and sentences from the last speakers, but the source does not tie the stress description to any particular kind of evidence.
morph.stmt: §1.1 p.1: 'Wargamay is a fairly typical Australian language with a suffixing, agglutinative structure and free word order'; nominals are 'root and a case inflection... Between root and inflection can come one or more derivational affixes' (§3.1 p.28) and verbs are 'Root (+ Derivational affix(es)) + Inflection' (§3.5.1 p.45); the complete List of Affixes (pp.142-143) contains only suffixes - no prefixes or proclitics of any kind.
